title: The 20-20-20 Rule
summary: A simple technique to reduce eye strain during extended screen use.

sections.title: What is the 20-20-20 rule?
sections.content: Every 20 minutes, look at something at least 20 feet (6 meters) away for at least 20 seconds. This gives your eye muscles a chance to relax from the constant near-focus required by screens.

sections.title: Why it matters
sections.content: When you focus on a screen, your ciliary muscles stay contracted for long periods. This sustained effort can lead to discomfort, headaches, and blurred vision. Regular distance viewing helps these muscles relax naturally.

sections.title: How to practice it
sections.content:
1. Set a timer for 20 minutes
2. When it提醒s you, look away from your screen
3. Find an object at least 20 feet away — a window view, a wall clock, or anything across the room
4. Focus on that object for at least 20 seconds
5. Blink naturally while doing this
6. Return to your screen

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
- Looking at something too close (less than 20 feet)
- Rushing through the 20 seconds
- Forgetting to blink during the break
- Only doing it when eyes already hurt

Choose a fixed focal point across the room
Blink naturally during each break

title: Healthy Blinking Habits
summary: Why blinking frequency drops during screen use and how to maintain healthy blink rates.

sections.title: How blinking works
sections.content: Most people blink 15 to 20 times per minute. Each blink spreads a thin layer of tears across the eye surface, keeping it moist and clear. When you focus on a screen, your blink rate can drop to 5 to 7 times per minute.

sections.title: Why screen use reduces blinking
sections.content: Concentration on digital content naturally suppresses the blink reflex. The smaller the screen and the closer the viewing distance, the more pronounced this effect tends to be. Extended periods without adequate blinking can leave eyes feeling dry and tired.

sections.title: Practical steps
sections.content:
1. Be conscious of your blink rate while working
2. Practice deliberate full blinks every few minutes
3. If your eyes feel dry, close them gently for 5 seconds
4. Keep artificial tears nearby if recommended by your eye-care professional
5. Position your screen slightly below eye level to reduce exposed eye surface

Full blinks are more effective than partial ones
Dry environments make this more important

title: Screen Distance and Viewing Comfort
summary: How monitor distance and angle affect your eyes and what adjustments help.

sections.title: Recommended distance
sections.content: Position your monitor at arm's length, roughly 50 to 70 cm (20 to 28 inches) from your eyes. This distance reduces the effort your eyes need to focus on the screen content.

sections.title: Screen angle
sections.content: Tilt your monitor slightly backward (10 to 20 degrees) and position the top of the screen at or slightly below eye level. This reduces neck strain and helps maintain a natural viewing angle.

sections.title: Adjustments that help
sections.content:
1. Measure your arm length and adjust monitor distance accordingly
2. Use a monitor stand or adjustable arm if needed
3. For laptops, consider an external monitor or laptop stand
4. Adjust font size rather than leaning closer to the screen
5. Re-check your setup periodically throughout the day

title: Workspace Lighting for Eye Comfort
summary: How ambient lighting and screen brightness interact to affect eye comfort.

sections.title: The lighting balance
sections.content: Your screen brightness should roughly match the ambient light around you. Working in a dark room with a bright screen, or in bright sunlight with a dim screen, forces your eyes to work harder to adapt.

sections.title: Reducing glare
sections.content: Glare from windows or overhead lights can cause you to squint or lean forward. Position your screen perpendicular to windows rather than facing them or having a window behind you.

sections.title: Practical adjustments
sections.content:
1. Set screen brightness to match your surroundings
2. Use blinds or curtains to control natural light
3. Position your monitor away from direct light sources
4. Consider a desk lamp with adjustable brightness for evening work
5. Use the night light or warm display setting in the evening

Position windows to the side, not behind or in front

title: Why Regular Screen Breaks Matter
summary: The physiological reasons breaks help and how to build sustainable break habits.

sections.title: What happens during extended screen use
sections.content: When you stare at a screen for long periods, several things happen: your blink rate decreases, your ciliary muscles stay contracted, your posture often deteriorates, and your eyes receive less varied visual stimulation. These factors combine to cause discomfort over time.

sections.title: How breaks help
sections.content: Short, regular breaks allow your eye muscles to relax, your blink rate to recover, and your posture to reset. Even a 20-second break every 20 minutes can make a meaningful difference in comfort over a work day.

sections.title: Building the habit
sections.content:
1. Use a timer or app to remind you at regular intervals
2. Stand up and look around during breaks
3. Combine screen breaks with light stretching
4. Make breaks a non-negotiable part of your workflow
5. Track your break consistency if it helps you stay accountable

quick_tips: Short, frequent breaks are better than occasional long ones
Combine breaks with standing or stretching

title: Understanding Digital Eye Strain
summary: What digital eye strain is, what causes it, and what you can do about it.

sections.title: What it is
sections.content: Digital eye strain, also called computer vision syndrome, refers to a group of symptoms that can occur after extended screen use. These may include dry eyes, blurred vision, headaches, and neck or shoulder discomfort.

sections.title: What causes it
sections.content: Reduced blinking, sustained near-focus, glare, poor screen positioning, and uncorrected vision problems can all contribute. It is not caused by screen light itself damaging the eyes, but by the way we use screens.

sections.title: What you can do
sections.content:
1. Follow the 20-20-20 rule
2. Blink consciously and fully
3. Adjust your screen distance and brightness
4. Take regular breaks
5. If symptoms persist, consult an eye-care professional

title: Building Better Focus Sessions
summary: How to structure work sessions that protect your eyes while maintaining productivity.

sections.title: Structured focus
sections.content: Working in focused blocks with built-in breaks is more sustainable than trying to power through hours without pausing. A common approach is 25 minutes of focused work followed by a 5-minute break.

sections.title: Combining focus with eye care
sections.content: Each break is an opportunity to look away from your screen, blink fully, and shift your focus to a distant object. This naturally integrates eye care into your workflow without adding extra steps.

sections.title: Getting started
sections.content:
1. Choose a focus duration (25 minutes is common)
2. Set a timer
3. Work without screen distractions
4. When the timer sounds, take a real break — look away, stand up, move
5. Return after 5 minutes and repeat

title: Nutrition and Eye Comfort
summary: How dietary choices may support eye comfort during regular screen use.

sections.title: What helps
sections.content: A balanced diet rich in omega-3 fatty acids, vitamins A, C, and E, and minerals like zinc may support overall eye comfort. Foods like leafy greens, fish, citrus fruits, and nuts are commonly recommended.

sections.title: Hydration matters
sections.content: Dehydration can reduce tear production, making dry eyes more likely. Drinking enough water throughout the day supports healthy tear films and overall comfort.

sections.title: Practical steps
sections.content:
1. Include leafy greens and colorful vegetables in your meals
2. Eat fish or nuts several times a week if possible
3. Keep water nearby and drink regularly
4. Avoid excessive caffeine, which can contribute to dehydration
5. For specific dietary advice, consult a healthcare professional

title: When to See an Eye-Care Professional
summary: Signs that warrant professional evaluation versus habits that self-resolve.

sections.title: When self-care is enough
sections.content: Mild, occasional discomfort that improves with breaks, blinking, and ergonomic adjustments is common and usually manageable with the habits described in this app. Most digital eye strain symptoms are temporary.

sections.title: When to seek professional advice
sections.content: Consider scheduling an appointment with an eye-care professional if you experience: persistent dry eyes that do not improve, frequent headaches, blurred vision that does not clear with rest, difficulty focusing, or any sudden changes in vision.

sections.title: What to expect
sections.content: An eye-care professional can evaluate your vision, check for underlying conditions, and provide personalized recommendations. Regular eye exams are recommended for all adults, even without symptoms.
